title: What a 1924 Laurelhurst Basement Taught Us About Finishing Old Portland Basements
description: Lessons from a 1924 Laurelhurst basement remodel in Portland: moisture control, interior drain tile, BDS permits, egress window code, radon testing, and materials that survive a wet climate.
coverAlt: Finished basement living space in a Southeast Portland remodel by Rip City Construction
html:
Last winter we finished the basement of a 1924 craftsman in Laurelhurst, a few blocks off NE Sandy. The lower level had spent a hundred years as a laundry room and paint-can storage. The owners wanted a family room, a guest bedroom, and a full bath, about 850 square feet of new living space. The project went well because we treated it as a moisture project first and a finish project second, the right order for almost every pre-1940 basement in inner Portland.

Our basement finishing and remodeling page covers what we build; this is the part that rarely fits there.

Start With Water, Not Finishes

The house had no drain tile; almost nothing built in Portland before 1950 does. The warning signs were clear: white chalky efflorescence on the north foundation wall, downspouts ending two feet from the concrete, and soil sloped toward the house. Efflorescence means water is moving through the wall. None of this kills a remodel, but all of it gets fixed before anyone frames a wall.

We extended the downspouts, regraded the side yard, and cut an interior perimeter drain along the footing that feeds a sealed sump basin with a battery backup pump. A dimpled drainage mat behind the new stud walls gives moisture a path to the drain instead of into the insulation. The rim joists got closed-cell spray foam; the old fiberglass batts stuffed against the concrete came out, because in this climate that is how you grow mold inside a wall.

Checks we run before quoting any basement finish:

  • Efflorescence or spalling on foundation walls
  • Musty odor within a day of heavy rain
  • Gutters, downspouts, and grade around the perimeter
  • A radon test result

Permits, Egress, and Ceiling Height in Portland

A finished basement with a bedroom in Portland is permitted work through the Bureau of Development Services, and there is no reasonable version of skipping it. The permit makes the bedroom legal sleeping space that an appraiser can count, and unpermitted basement work is one of the first things a buyer's inspector flags when you sell.

Egress surprises most homeowners. Any basement bedroom needs an emergency escape opening: a window with at least 5.7 square feet of net clear opening and a sill no more than 44 inches off the floor. In a 1924 foundation that means cutting a larger opening in concrete and setting a window well outside, work that has to be in the plan from day one. We did the same thing on a recent basement remodel on SE Clay Street, where a new egress window turned a storage room into a legal guest bedroom.

Ceiling height is the other constraint. Habitable basement space in an existing Portland home generally needs 6 feet 8 inches of clear height, measured under beams and duct soffits. This house gave us 7 feet 4 inches, so we planned duct runs early and kept the ceiling above the line. Houses with less headroom sometimes need the slab lowered, which changes the budget conversation entirely.

Materials That Survive a Portland Basement

Nine months of rain changes what good material means below grade. We used paperless fiberglass-mat drywall instead of paper-faced board, luxury vinyl plank rated for below-grade installation, and PVC baseboard that cannot wick water. Bottom plates are pressure-treated lumber over a foam gasket, so wood never touches raw concrete. The new bath got the same porcelain tile and waterproofing approach we use in our bathroom and tile work, plus an exhaust fan vented outside.

We also tested for radon before closing up the walls. Much of inner Portland sits on gravel deposited by the Missoula Floods, so basement radon readings here are worth taking seriously. This test came back under the action level, but a mitigation rough-in would have cost almost nothing at rough stage.

What We Would Tell Any Portland Homeowner

Budget for water management before finishes, design egress and ceiling height before layout, and pick materials that assume damp air from November through May. Do those three things and an old Portland basement is some of the best square footage in the house. Skip them and you have built a very expensive mold terrarium. If you want a straight answer on your own basement, start a conversation with our team, or see how these details look in our Portland remodeling projects.

FAQ

Do I need a permit to finish my basement in Portland?

Yes. Finished basement work, especially a new bedroom or bathroom, is permitted through the City of Portland Bureau of Development Services. Fees are a small fraction of the budget, and permitted space counts as finished square footage at resale.

How do I know if my basement is dry enough to finish?

Watch it through one wet season if you can. Fix gutters, downspouts, and grading first, then look for efflorescence or musty smells after heavy rain. If the foundation still shows moisture, an interior perimeter drain and sealed sump usually solve it, and that work is far cheaper before framing than after.

Can a finished basement become an ADU later?

Often, yes. A basement ADU needs its own egress, adequate ceiling height, and usually a separate entrance, so it pays to rough in plumbing and electrical with that future in mind. Our ADU and home addition work includes basement conversions, and we can tell you in one visit if your basement qualifies.

title: Bathroom Remodeling in Portland: What to Expect From a Local Contractor
description: What a Portland bathroom remodel really involves: cost drivers, a two to four week timeline, older-home surprises, moisture-smart materials, and the questions to ask before hiring a contractor.
coverAlt: Remodeled bathroom with custom tile work in a Northeast Portland home by Rip City Construction
html:
A bathroom remodel sounds simple until you start pulling up old tile and find out what's behind it. Portland homes, especially the older ones scattered through Hawthorne, Richmond, and the surrounding neighborhoods, often hide a few surprises once the walls open up. Knowing what a solid remodel actually involves, and who you're trusting to do it, matters more than picking a tile pattern off Pinterest.

Rip City Construction & Remodeling LLC has been doing bathroom work out of our shop on SE Hawthorne Blvd for a while now, and the questions we get from homeowners tend to repeat themselves. This post walks through the practical side of a Portland bathroom remodel: what drives cost, what to plan for, and where things typically go sideways if nobody's paying attention.

Why Bathrooms Are Different From Other Remodels

Bathrooms pack more systems into a small footprint than almost any other room in the house. Plumbing, electrical, ventilation, and waterproofing all have to work together in a space that might be eight feet by ten feet. That's part of why bathroom remodeling is its own category of work rather than something tacked onto a general punch list.

Older Portland homes add another layer. Galvanized pipe, undersized exhaust fans, and subfloor damage from decades of slow leaks are common finds once demo starts. A contractor who's done this kind of work around the city knows to budget time and flexibility for what's behind the wall, not just what's on the mood board.

What Goes Into a Portland Bathroom Remodel

Our bathroom remodeling projects usually fall into a few categories: full gut renovations, shower and tub conversions, and layout changes where a wall moves to make room for a larger vanity or a walk-in shower. Tile selection is a big part of the conversation early on, since it affects both the look and the long-term durability of the space. Custom tile work, vanity installs, and shower pans built to handle daily use are where most of the budget and most of the decisions live.

Layout upgrades come up often too, especially in houses built before accessibility and storage were top of mind. Moving a toilet a few inches, widening a doorway, or swapping a tub for a curbless shower can change how a bathroom functions without expanding its footprint. These changes take more planning than people expect, since plumbing lines and venting don't always move as easily as drywall.

Timeline and Process

A typical bathroom remodel in Portland runs anywhere from two to four weeks once demo starts, depending on scope and whether any structural or plumbing surprises show up. The early phase, before a single hammer swings, matters just as much: selecting materials, finalizing the layout, and getting a clear scope of work written down so there's no guessing later. We walk every project through design, material selection, and a realistic schedule before construction begins, because vague timelines are where trust in a contractor starts to erode.

During construction, communication is what separates a smooth project from a frustrating one. Homeowners should expect regular updates, especially if something unexpected turns up once tile or drywall comes down. Good contractors flag problems early instead of letting them pile up until the end.

A Small Story From the Field

One remodel near Hawthorne started as a straightforward tile and vanity swap, until the crew pulled the old tub and found the subfloor had been soft for years under a slow leak nobody knew about. The schedule shifted by about a week to replace the damaged framing and subfloor before any new tile went in. The homeowner ended up glad it was caught then instead of a year later, which is usually how these things go once you're actually inside the walls.

Bathrooms, Kitchens, and the Rest of the House

Bathroom remodels rarely happen in a vacuum. Homeowners planning a bathroom update often end up asking about related work at the same time, whether that's a kitchen remodel down the hall, finishing an unfinished basement into usable space with basement remodeling, or adding square footage altogether through an ADU or home addition. It's worth mentioning all of it up front during the first conversation with a contractor, even if the bathroom is the only project on the table right now. Scheduling and budgeting get easier when the bigger picture is on the table from day one.

For property owners handling tenant improvements or office space rather than a residence, commercial bathroom and build-out work falls under a different process. Our commercial remodeling projects follow similar principles around durability and code compliance, just scaled to a different use case.

Picking the Right Materials for Portland's Climate

Moisture management is non-negotiable in a Portland bathroom. The region's wet winters mean ventilation and waterproofing can't be an afterthought, especially behind tile and around shower pans. Choosing the right backer board, waterproofing membrane, and exhaust fan sizing isn't glamorous work, but it's the difference between a bathroom that lasts fifteen years and one that needs tile repair in five.

Material choices also affect maintenance down the line. Natural stone looks great but needs sealing; porcelain tile handles moisture and wear with less upkeep. A contractor should walk through these tradeoffs honestly rather than just pushing whatever's trending, since the homeowner is the one living with the choice long after the crew packs up.

For homeowners thinking beyond the bathroom toward whole-home efficiency, it's also worth asking about solar panel maintenance if panels are already on the roof or in the plan, since keeping them clean affects how much they actually produce. We work alongside Northwest Solar Clean on projects where homeowners are tackling both remodeling and solar upkeep at the same time, and it's a natural pairing for anyone already investing in their home's long-term performance.

Questions to Ask Before Hiring a Contractor

A few questions tend to separate a contractor who knows bathroom work from one who's guessing. Ask how they handle unexpected issues once demo starts, since every older home has at least one surprise waiting. Ask for a clear written scope of work rather than a verbal estimate, and ask how they sequence trades like plumbing and electrical so nothing gets covered up before it's inspected.

It also helps to ask about past projects in your specific neighborhood. Contractors who've worked across Portland's older housing stock, from Hawthorne to the surrounding streets, tend to recognize patterns in plumbing age, foundation quirks, and permitting requirements that an out-of-area crew might miss entirely.

Getting Started

If a bathroom remodel has been sitting on a list for a while, the best next step is usually just a conversation. Rip City Construction & Remodeling LLC is based at 7648 SE Hawthorne Blvd in Portland and keeps office hours Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM. Reach out at (971) 344-3806 or info@ripcityconstruction.com to talk through scope, budget, and timeline before anything gets scheduled.

FAQ

How long does a bathroom remodel take in Portland?

Most full bathroom remodels take two to four weeks once demolition begins, though older homes with hidden plumbing or structural issues can extend that. Ask your contractor for a realistic range rather than a single fixed date.

What's the biggest cost driver in a bathroom remodel?

Tile, custom shower builds, and plumbing or layout changes typically drive cost more than fixtures alone. Moving plumbing lines or widening a doorway adds labor that a simple surface refresh wouldn't require.

Do older Portland homes need special attention during a remodel?

Yes, older homes often have galvanized pipe, undersized ventilation, or subfloor damage that isn't visible until demo starts. A contractor familiar with Portland's housing stock will budget time and flexibility for these kinds of finds.

Can I combine a bathroom remodel with other home projects?

Many homeowners pair bathroom work with a kitchen remodel, basement finishing, or an ADU addition to save on scheduling and planning overhead. It's worth mentioning any other projects during your first conversation with a contractor, even if they're not ready to start yet.

title: How Much Does an ADU Cost in Portland, Oregon?
description: What really drives ADU costs in Portland: detached builds vs. garage and basement conversions, permitting and system development charges, lot slope and utility access, and how finishes change the number.
coverAlt: Detached accessory dwelling unit built in Portland by Rip City Construction
html:
At our office on SE Hawthorne Blvd, this is the question we hear before almost anything else. Somebody has a side yard, an old garage, or a basement that never gets used, and they want a dollar figure before they even think about layout. The honest answer is that ADU costs in Portland swing widely from project to project, and anyone who gives you a flat number without seeing your lot is guessing.

That said, there are patterns. After years of building ADU and home addition projects across Portland, we can walk you through what actually moves the needle on price, so you can ask better questions and budget with your eyes open.

What Actually Drives the Price

Square footage matters, but it's not the only factor, and sometimes not even the biggest one. Foundation type, utility connections, roofline complexity, and how far the unit sits from existing sewer and water lines all affect cost before a single cabinet goes in. A detached unit on a flat, easy-access lot in outer Portland behaves very differently, budget-wise, than a similar-sized unit squeezed onto a sloped lot in a denser neighborhood close to the city core.

Labor and material costs shift with the market too. Lumber, windows, and fixtures have all seen price swings over the past few years, which is part of why we always recommend getting a current, project-specific estimate rather than relying on a number you read somewhere last year.

Detached Builds vs. Conversions

A brand-new detached ADU, built from the ground up, generally costs more than converting existing space because you're paying for a full foundation, new framing, a full roof system, and all-new utility runs. A garage conversion or a basement buildout can come in lower because some of the structural shell already exists. We handle both, and the right path depends on what you've already got on your property.

If you've got an unfinished basement instead of yard space to build on, it's worth comparing that option directly against a detached unit. Our basement finishing work often ends up being the more budget-friendly route to added living space, though it comes with its own set of considerations around ceiling height, egress windows, and moisture control that a detached build doesn't have to deal with.

Permits, Code, and Portland-Specific Factors

Portland's ADU permitting process has its own quirks, and the city has made changes over the years around system development charges and allowed unit sizes. Permitting timelines affect your overall project schedule and, indirectly, your budget, since longer timelines mean more exposure to material price changes. Older Portland neighborhoods also tend to have mature trees, narrow access points, and sewer lines that were never designed with a second dwelling unit in mind, all of which can add cost that doesn't show up in a simple per-square-foot estimate.

Lot slope is another one people underestimate. A lot that drops several feet from street to backyard, which describes a lot of Portland's east side, often needs retaining work or a different foundation approach than a flat lot would. None of this is meant to scare anyone off. It's meant to explain why two ADUs that look identical on paper can land at very different prices once the site work starts.

Finishes Change the Number More Than People Expect

Once the shell and systems are in place, finish level is where a lot of the remaining budget flexibility lives. A simple, efficient kitchen layout costs less than a full custom build with stone countertops and custom cabinetry, and the same is true in the bathroom. If you're weighing finish options for an ADU kitchen, it's worth looking at how we approach kitchen remodeling in Portland, since a lot of the same cabinetry and layout decisions apply at a smaller scale. The same goes for bathroom and tile work, where tile selection and fixture quality can swing a bathroom budget significantly even within a small ADU footprint.

Our advice is usually to spend where you'll feel it daily, good lighting, a layout that works, durable surfaces, and pull back on anything purely decorative if the budget is tight. Those choices add up fast, and they're the ones a contractor can actually help you prioritize once real numbers are on the table.

Why Costs Vary So Much Project to Project

We've seen ADU budgets land all over the map, even on units with similar square footage, because site conditions and finish choices compound each other. A detached unit with full utility trenching, a steep driveway for access, and higher-end finishes will naturally cost more than a garage conversion with existing utility stubs and a simpler finish package. This is exactly why we walk every property in person before giving numbers. We also work alongside other local trades when a project needs specialized design input, and for certain custom design questions we'll point clients toward Rolly Builders as a trusted resource in the area.

One pattern we notice every year is a wave of inquiries in early spring, right as people start picturing their yard with something built on it instead of just grass. We had someone walk in during our regular Monday morning hours, coffee in hand, who'd been eyeing a detached garage for an ADU conversion for two winters straight before finally coming in to ask what it would actually take. That's a common story here, people sit with the idea a long time before they're ready to get real numbers.

Getting an Accurate Number for Your Lot

The only way to get a cost figure you can actually plan around is to have someone walk your property, look at your existing utility access, check the slope, and talk through what you want the unit for, whether that's rental income, a place for family, or just more breathing room on your lot. General cost ranges floating around online rarely account for Portland's specific permitting rules or the condition of an individual lot, so treat those numbers as a starting point for a conversation, not a budget.

If you're in the early stages of figuring out whether an ADU, an addition, or a basement conversion makes more sense for your property, reach out during our regular hours, Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 5 PM. We're at 7648 SE Hawthorne Blvd in Portland, and you can call us at (971) 344-3806 or email info@ripcityconstruction.com to set up a time to look at your lot in person.

FAQ

Is a detached ADU always more expensive than a conversion?

Usually, yes, because a detached unit needs a new foundation, full framing, and new utility runs that a conversion can often avoid. Garage and basement conversions typically cost less since part of the structure already exists.

Does Portland charge extra fees for ADUs?

Portland has its own permitting process and system development charges that can affect your total project cost. These fees and requirements change periodically, so it's best to ask for current figures when you're budgeting a specific project.

Can an ADU be built on a sloped Portland lot?

Yes, but sloped lots often require retaining work or a modified foundation approach, which adds cost compared to a flat lot. A site walk is the best way to understand how much a slope will affect your specific budget.

Should I convert my basement instead of building a detached ADU?

It depends on your basement's ceiling height, egress options, and moisture conditions, as well as how much yard space you have. Comparing both options side by side, ideally with a contractor who handles both, is the best way to decide which makes more financial sense for your property.

title: What Does a Home Addition Cost in Portland, Oregon?
description: What really drives home addition costs in Portland: foundation tie-ins on older houses, roofline complexity, plumbing and electrical in the new space, lot access, and BDS permitting time.
coverAlt: Finished home addition on a Southeast Portland house built by Rip City Construction
html:
Every homeowner who calls us about a home addition asks the same question in the first thirty seconds: what's this going to cost? It's a fair question, and it's also the hardest one to answer without actually looking at the house. Portland lots, older framing, sloped yards in the hills, and the city's permitting process all push numbers around more than people expect. This article won't hand you a magic number, because nobody honest can do that over the phone, but it will walk through what actually moves the price up or down.

What Drives the Price of a Home Addition

Square footage gets all the attention, but it's rarely the biggest variable. Foundation work usually is. If your addition needs new footings tied into a house built in the 1920s or 1940s, which describes a huge chunk of Portland's housing stock, that connection work takes time and careful engineering. Roofline complexity matters too. A simple bump-out with a shed roof is a different job than a second-story addition that has to tie into existing trusses and match the original pitch.

Then there's what's inside the new space. A bedroom and a closet cost a lot less per square foot than a full bathroom or a kitchenette, because plumbing and electrical rough-in add labor and materials that framing alone doesn't. Site access plays a role as well. Some Portland lots, especially in neighborhoods like Sellwood or parts of Southeast with narrow driveways, make it harder to get equipment and materials where they need to go, which can add time to a schedule even when the square footage is modest.

Finally, permitting and inspections take longer than people expect in this city. Portland's Bureau of Development Services reviews structural additions carefully, and that review time is part of the real cost of the project even though it doesn't show up as a line item on your contract.

Addition vs. ADU: Which Fits Your Lot

Not every project that starts as an addition stays an addition. Some homeowners come in wanting more square footage attached to the main house, then realize a detached unit makes more sense for their goals, especially if rental income or a space for aging parents is part of the plan. We cover that comparison in detail over on our ADU and home additions page, since the two options often get weighed against each other during the same conversation. The short version: additions make sense when you want connected living space, like a larger primary suite or an expanded family room, while a detached unit makes more sense when privacy or separate utilities matter.

Either way, the zoning and setback rules that apply to your specific lot in Portland will shape what's even possible before cost enters the conversation. That's worth sorting out early, before you fall in love with a floor plan that your lot can't actually support.

A Walk Through Our Hawthorne Office

We're set up at 7648 SE Hawthorne Blvd, and because we keep regular hours Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 5 PM, we get a fair number of people who just stop in with a sketch on a napkin or photos on their phone. One pattern we see almost every spring: a homeowner walks in wanting to talk through adding a second story over an existing single-story footprint, usually because their family outgrew the house but they don't want to move out of the neighborhood. Those conversations almost always start with the same question about cost, and they almost always end with us scheduling a site visit, because a real number requires actually seeing the roof, the foundation, and the yard.

Ways to Keep Costs in Line

There are a few decisions that genuinely affect the bottom line without cutting corners on quality. Matching your addition's finishes to what you already have, rather than upgrading everything in the existing house to match the new space, keeps the project scoped to what you actually came in for. Choosing a simpler roofline where it won't hurt the look of the house saves on framing complexity. And being flexible on exact cabinetry or fixture brands, while still landing in the quality range you want, gives your contractor room to manage material costs without compromising the build.

It also helps to think about the whole house, not just the addition, before construction starts. If an addition is going to open up a wall near your kitchen, for example, that might be the right moment to also look at kitchen remodeling while the walls are already open, rather than doing it as a separate project two years later. The same logic applies to bathrooms. If your addition includes a new bath or touches plumbing near an existing one, it's worth asking about bathroom remodeling at the same time, since combining the work can reduce some of the overlap in labor and permitting.

We also work alongside other local trades and firms when a project calls for specialized scope outside our usual lane, and we'll sometimes point homeowners toward Cornerstone Renovations for work that falls outside what we handle directly. Portland's remodeling community is smaller than people think, and a good referral network usually means a better outcome for the homeowner.

What to Expect When You Call Rip City Construction

When you reach out to us, the first step is almost always a conversation about what you're trying to solve, not a quote. Are you adding square footage because your family grew, because you want a home office that isn't also a dining table, or because you're planning ahead for a parent moving in? That answer shapes whether an addition, a basement conversion, or something else entirely is the right call. If your house has unused below-grade space, for instance, basement finishing sometimes solves the same square-footage problem as an addition for a fraction of the structural work, since the foundation and roof are already in place.

From there, we schedule a site visit, walk the property, and talk through rough budget ranges based on what we see. A detailed estimate follows once we understand the scope, and that's when real numbers start to take shape. We also take on larger-scale work, including commercial remodeling for tenant improvements, so if your project is a mixed-use building or a live-work space, that's a conversation we can have too.

The honest answer to the cost question is that it depends on your specific house, your lot, and what you want the new space to do for your family. Anyone who gives you a firm number before seeing the property is guessing. What we can promise is a straightforward estimate once we've actually looked, and a schedule that matches what we tell you up front.

FAQ

How much does a home addition cost in Portland, Oregon?

Costs vary widely based on foundation work, roofline complexity, and whether plumbing or electrical is involved in the new space. The only reliable way to get a real number is a site visit, which you can schedule by calling (971) 344-3806 or reaching out through our contact page.

How long does a home addition take from start to finish?

Timelines depend on permitting review with the city and the scope of structural work, so there's no single answer that applies to every house. A detailed estimate will include a project-specific schedule once the scope is finalized.

Is a home addition cheaper than building an ADU in Portland?

It depends on the goal. Additions often cost less when they're adding simple living space connected to the existing house, while detached ADUs involve separate utilities and foundations that can add cost but offer more flexibility for rental income or separate living.

Do I need a permit for a home addition in Portland?

Yes, structural additions require review and permitting through the City of Portland's Bureau of Development Services. Rip City Construction handles that process as part of managing your project from design through completion.
